title: When to Use MCP vs Raw Function Calling

seo.title: MCP vs Raw Function Calling: When to use which
seo.description: Understand the latency tradeoffs and architectural differences between standard LLM function calling and the Model Context Protocol.

glossary.definition: The standard process of directly passing a hardcoded JSON schema to an LLM provider's API (e.g., in the OpenAI `tools` array) without any intermediary protocol.
The multi-step handshake MCP uses to discover tools dynamically before the LLM can even be invoked.

hook.scenario: You're building a simple, single-purpose Slack bot that checks the weather. You decide to spin up a dedicated MCP server in a Docker container just to expose the weather API to your LLM, adding complexity and latency.
hook.question: A developer building a single-purpose weather chatbot decides to spin up a separate MCP server instance instead of passing the weather schema directly to the LLM. Why is this structurally inefficient?

mental_model.intuition: Raw function calling is a direct, hardcoded wire. MCP is a universal switchboard.
mental_model.description: You built the raw execution loop in the Function/tool calling lesson. You already know how to pass a JSON schema to `client.chat.completions.create`. MCP doesn't replace that underlying mechanism; it wraps it in a switchboard. MCP is built for runtime discovery and scaling across many models and tools. But if you have a closed, single-purpose app, that switchboard is just overhead. Direct APIs are faster and cheaper.

sections.body: In standard function calling, you hardcode the schema and send it directly in the LLM's `tools` array. The model replies instantly with a tool call. It's a single network hop. It's extremely fast and requires zero extra infrastructure.
sections.recap: Raw function calling is a direct, single-hop integration with zero protocol overhead.

sections.body: MCP introduces a negotiation handshake. Before the Host can invoke the LLM, it must send an `initialize` request to the MCP Server, wait for the response, send a `tools/list` request to discover capabilities, and wait for that response. Only then does it pass the schemas to the LLM.
sections.recap: MCP requires a multi-step JSON-RPC negotiation phase before inference begins.

sections.body: This handshake means MCP inherently introduces latency. It is structurally impossible for MCP to be faster than a raw, direct function call. If a developer benchmarks an MCP server against a raw API call and sees a 50ms increase, the server isn't broken—that is the mathematical reality of protocol negotiation.
sections.recap: MCP adds latency; it does not reduce it. Its benefit is architectural scalability, not execution speed.

sections.body: So when does MCP earn its complexity? Scale. If you are building an open ecosystem (like an AI IDE) that needs to dynamically discover tools from third-party plugins at runtime, MCP is mandatory. If you are integrating 10 different tools across 4 different LLMs, the M×N integration problem justifies the switchboard.
sections.recap: MCP is for open ecosystems, runtime discovery, and massive multi-tool scale.

sections.body: Conversely, if you are building a closed system—like a dedicated customer support bot with exactly two internal APIs and one LLM—you should use standard raw function calling. Adding an MCP server to a closed, single-purpose system is pure over-engineering.
sections.recap: For single-purpose, closed systems, raw function calling is definitively faster and cheaper.

code_snippets.title: Raw Function Calling: The single network hop
code_snippets.explanation: Zero discovery overhead. You know the tool exists, you format it perfectly, and you send it directly to the model. This is the lowest possible latency.

code_snippets.title: The MCP overhead: Multi-step negotiation
code_snippets.code:
# To get the same result, the Host must first negotiate:
# 1. Host -> Server: initialize
# 2. Server -> Host: initialize_result
# 3. Host -> Server: tools/list
# 4. Server -> Host: tools_result (containing the schemas)

# 5. NOW the Host translates and calls the LLM provider
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=user_messages,
    tools=translated_mcp_tools
)
code_snippets.explanation: Steps 1 through 4 add network latency before the LLM even sees the prompt. This overhead is only justified if you don't know what tools are available until runtime.

common_mistakes.title: Assuming MCP replaces all function calling
common_mistakes.explanation: Because of industry hype, developers assume MCP is universally superior and should replace standard OpenAI function calling everywhere. Reality: MCP is built for runtime discovery and standardisation across many tools. For a single, closed-system integration, a direct API call with native function calling is structurally faster, cheaper, and less complex.

common_mistakes.title: Expecting MCP to reduce LLM latency
common_mistakes.explanation: Developers assume standardisation equals performance optimization, expecting their LLM to generate faster because the tools use MCP. Reality: MCP actually introduces latency overhead due to the required negotiation handshakes (`initialize`, `tools/list`). If you see a latency increase when switching to MCP, your code isn't broken; that's the cost of the protocol.

recall_questions.q: What operational and latency overhead does the Model Context Protocol introduce compared to raw function calling?
recall_questions.answer: MCP requires a multi-step JSON-RPC negotiation handshake (`initialize`, `tools/list`) to dynamically discover tools before the Host can invoke the LLM, adding distinct network latency steps.

recall_questions.q: At what architectural scale does MCP explicitly earn its complexity?
recall_questions.answer: MCP earns its complexity in open ecosystems (where tools must be discovered at runtime from third-party plugins) or at massive scale (where the M×N problem of integrating many models with many tools becomes unmanageable).

recall_questions.q: A developer benchmarks an MCP server against a raw function call, sees a 50ms increase in latency with MCP, and assumes their server code is broken. Are they correct?
recall_questions.answer: No. The server isn't broken. The 50ms latency increase is the mathematical reality of the protocol's required negotiation handshakes compared to a direct, hardcoded API call.

recall_questions.q: A developer building a single-purpose weather chatbot decides to spin up a separate MCP server instance instead of passing the weather API schema directly to the LLM's tool array. Why is this a poor architectural choice?
recall_questions.answer: It is over-engineering. For a single, closed-system integration where the tools are known in advance, a direct API call with raw function calling is definitively faster, cheaper, and structurally simpler.

oa_questions.question: How is MCP different from a regular REST API?
oa_questions.answer: A regular REST API integration (like raw function calling) involves hardcoding the specific tool schema and sending it directly to the LLM in a single hop. MCP is a dynamic protocol that requires the client to negotiate a connection and actively query the server to discover its capabilities at runtime before translating them to the LLM.
oa_questions.approach: Contrast hardcoded schemas (REST/Function Calling) with dynamic runtime discovery (MCP). Highlight the latency tradeoff.

oa_questions.question: When would you choose raw function calling over MCP?
oa_questions.answer: I would choose raw function calling when building a single-purpose, closed system where all tools are known in advance (like a dedicated customer support bot). Implementing MCP in this scenario adds unnecessary negotiation latency and infrastructure overhead without providing the runtime discovery benefits that justify the protocol.
oa_questions.approach: Highlight the overhead of MCP's negotiation handshakes. Position MCP as a solution for open ecosystems, not simple closed scripts.
